title: Cold email sequence
summary: A short series of cold emails that introduces your business to a new prospect and asks for a reply.
deliverable: A sequence of cold emails with subject lines, send timing, two variants of the first email, and a short note on who to send it to.

spec_fields.label: Who are you writing to?
spec_fields.help: Job title, industry and company size.

spec_fields.label: Proof you can use
spec_fields.help: Results, customer names or numbers we may quote.

spec_fields.label: Who is sending? Name and role

rubric.text: Nothing is invented. Every result, customer name, number and claim comes from the brief.
rubric.pass_rule: No number, customer, result or claim appears that is not in the brief or plain knowledge about the buyer's own offer.

rubric.text: Each email speaks to the stated target and problem, not to everyone.
rubric.pass_rule: The first email names the target's role or industry and the problem within the first two sentences.

rubric.text: Each email asks for one clear next step that matches the goal.
rubric.pass_rule: Every email ends with exactly one ask, and the ask matches the goal field.

rubric.text: Emails are short and read like a person wrote them.
rubric.pass_rule: Each email body is 120 words or fewer, with no sentence over 25 words, and none uses phrases like 'I hope this finds you well' or 'game-changing'.

rubric.text: Each follow-up adds a new reason to reply instead of repeating the first.
rubric.pass_rule: Each follow-up email uses a different angle, proof point or question from the one before it.

baseline_prompt: You are an expert B2B cold email copywriter. Write a cold email sequence for the business described below. Include subject lines, the send timing between emails, and two versions of the first email. Keep each email under 120 words, speak to one specific reader, ask for one next step, and make each follow-up add something new. Use only facts and proof given in the brief. Do not invent results, customers or numbers. Avoid filler openers and hype words.
not_for: Spam or emails to purchased or scraped lists
Fake names, fake referrals or pretending to know the reader
Claims about money, health or legal results the buyer cannot prove

sample_briefs.text: We run a 6-person bookkeeping firm for dental practices in Ohio. We want a 4-email sequence to practice owners. We save them about 5 hours a month, and we have 14 dental clients. Goal is a 15-minute call.

I sell cold-chain temperature loggers to small food distributors. The buyer is usually the operations manager. They fail audits when records are missing. Our loggers email a report each day. Want 5 emails, direct tone, goal is a free trial unit.

Our agency builds Shopify stores for outdoor gear brands doing $1M to $5M a year. Need a 3-email sequence to founders. Case study: we cut one client's checkout steps from 5 to 3 (name is Ridgeline Packs, they allow us to say that). Goal is a reply.

We offer fractional HR for startups with 10 to 50 staff, $1,800 a month. Writing to founders who have no HR person. We handle contracts, onboarding and policy. No case studies yet. 4 emails, friendly, goal is booking a call.

demand_sources.note: Rate guide shows cold outreach at $100 to $350 per email and $300 to $1,000 per sequence. Cold outreach is one of the most-bought writing jobs.
Rate table by deliverable: email sequence $500 to $5,000, product description $25 to $250 each, case study $1,200 to $2,000, article $250 to $800.

title: LinkedIn outreach messages
summary: Connection requests and follow-up messages for LinkedIn that start real sales conversations.
deliverable: A connection request note, three follow-up messages, a reply guide for common answers, and short variants for different buyer roles.

spec_fields.label: Who are you messaging?
spec_fields.help: Job title, industry, company size.

spec_fields.label: Sender's role and background
spec_fields.help: One or two lines for the writer to match your voice.

rubric.text: Nothing is invented. No fake shared contacts, results, quotes or customer names.
rubric.pass_rule: No claim, mutual connection, number or customer appears that is not in the brief.

rubric.text: Messages fit LinkedIn length and manners.
rubric.pass_rule: Connection note is 300 characters or fewer; each follow-up is 90 words or fewer.

rubric.text: The first contact builds a reason to talk before selling.
rubric.pass_rule: The connection note and first follow-up do not ask for a call or push the offer in the first message.

rubric.text: Each follow-up has one clear, low-pressure ask that matches the goal.
rubric.pass_rule: Each follow-up ends with one ask, and the final one matches the goal field.

rubric.text: The reply guide covers likely answers.
rubric.pass_rule: The guide gives a suggested reply for at least four answers, including 'not interested' and 'send me info'.

baseline_prompt: You are an experienced B2B social-selling coach. Write a LinkedIn outreach set for the business below: one connection request note (300 characters or fewer), three follow-up messages (90 words or fewer each), and a guide with suggested replies to likely answers such as not interested and send me info. Do not pitch in the first message. Use only the facts and proof in the brief. Do not invent mutual connections, results or names.
not_for: Fake profiles or pretending to know the reader
Messages built on scraped or purchased data

sample_briefs.text: I run a payroll service for restaurants with 5 to 30 staff. I want to reach restaurant owners and general managers on LinkedIn. Flat fee of $4 per employee a month. Goal is a call. Friendly tone.
Our company sells forklift safety training to warehouse managers in Texas. Training takes 2 hours on site. We want messages that get a reply, not a hard sell.

I'm a freelance product designer who wants to reach heads of product at early SaaS startups. I redesign onboarding flows. I cut sign-up steps for a client from 7 to 4 (client name stays private). Goal is a short chat.
We sell a tool that turns Zoom calls into meeting notes for law firm office managers. Buyers worry about privacy. We store nothing after 30 days. Want two versions, one formal, one casual.

demand_sources.note: Rate guide shows cold outreach at $100 to $350 per email and $300 to $1,000 per sequence. Cold outreach is one of the most-bought writing jobs.
Rate table by experience: single email $75 to $175 (junior), email sequence of 5 to 7 emails $500 to $1,000 (junior), landing page $300 to $750.

title: Sales call script
summary: A call script with opening, questions, talking points and a close, for discovery or demo calls.
deliverable: A call script with an opening, discovery questions, a short pitch, answers to common questions, a close, and voicemail and gatekeeper lines.

spec_fields.label: Who is on the call?
spec_fields.help: Role, industry, usual worries.

spec_fields.label: Price range, if you share it on calls
Your sales steps after this call

rubric.text: Nothing is invented. Prices, results, features and customer names come from the brief.
rubric.pass_rule: No price, feature, result or customer name appears that is not in the brief.

rubric.text: The script finds the buyer's need before pitching.
rubric.pass_rule: At least five open questions appear before any pitch section, and they cover the problem, current approach, cost of the problem and who decides.

rubric.text: The script suits the stated call type and length.
rubric.pass_rule: Opening and flow match the call_type field, and total talk time fits the call length when given.

rubric.text: The script ends with a clear next step tied to the goal.
rubric.pass_rule: A closing section asks for the step in the goal field and gives words for a yes and for a not now.

rubric.text: Lines sound like speech, not writing.
rubric.pass_rule: No spoken line is over 25 words, and lines are marked as what to say versus notes to the caller.

baseline_prompt: You are a veteran sales coach. Write a call script for the business and call type below. Include an opening, open discovery questions that come before any pitch, a short pitch, answers to likely questions, a close that asks for the stated next step (with words for yes and not now), and voicemail and gatekeeper lines if it is a cold call. Mark spoken lines separately from notes. Use only the facts given. Do not invent prices, results or customers.
not_for: Deceptive tactics such as fake urgency or posing as someone else
Robocall or auto-dialler scripts that skip consent rules
Scripts for regulated advice such as investments, insurance or medical
Calling lists the buyer bought without consent

sample_briefs.text: We sell commercial cleaning to small offices in Denver. Our reps cold call office managers. Contracts start at $600 a month. I want a 3-minute cold call script with a voicemail.

We sell a scheduling app to physical therapy clinics. After a demo request, our rep runs a 30-minute discovery call with the clinic owner. Main worry for owners is no-shows. Plans start at $79 a month per clinic.

Our firm installs rooftop solar for homeowners in Arizona. Leads come from a web form. The caller needs a 10-minute qualifying call script and a way to book a site visit. We never quote final prices on the phone.
I sell used heavy trucks to small construction firms. Most buyers call us after seeing a listing. I need a script for the first inbound call that finds out what they need and sets a viewing.

demand_sources.note: Rate table by deliverable: email sequence $500 to $5,000, product description $25 to $250 each, case study $1,200 to $2,000, article $250 to $800.

title: Objection handling guide
summary: Short, honest answers to the objections your buyers raise most, written for your reps to use.
deliverable: For each objection: what the buyer really means, a short reply, one follow-up question, and what not to say. Plus a one-page cheat sheet.

spec_fields.label: Objections you hear
spec_fields.help: Add real ones if you have them. We add common ones.

spec_fields.label: Your pricing and what is flexible

rubric.text: Nothing is invented. Facts, savings, features and competitor claims come from the brief.
rubric.pass_rule: No number, feature, result or competitor claim appears that is not in the brief.

rubric.text: Every objection the buyer listed is answered.
rubric.pass_rule: Each item in objection_list has its own entry.

rubric.text: Replies show the rep understands the worry before answering.
rubric.pass_rule: Each entry has a 'what they mean' line and the reply starts by acknowledging the concern.

rubric.text: Replies do not pressure or mislead.
rubric.pass_rule: No reply uses fake urgency, hides a known limit, or runs down a competitor without a fact from the brief.

rubric.text: Replies are short enough to say aloud.
rubric.pass_rule: Each reply is 60 words or fewer and each entry includes one follow-up question.

baseline_prompt: You are a sales trainer. Write an objection handling guide for the business below. For each objection give what the buyer really means, a short reply (60 words or fewer), one follow-up question, and what not to say. Cover every objection the buyer listed and add the most common ones for this kind of buyer. End with a one-page cheat sheet. Be honest: no fake urgency, no unproven claims, nothing invented.
not_for: Hiding fees, limits or contract terms
Regulated sales such as insurance or investments

sample_briefs.text: We sell a $199 a month CRM for real estate teams. Reps hear: too expensive, we already use spreadsheets, and my agents will not use it. We offer a 30-day free trial and free setup.
I run a landscaping company and sell yearly lawn care plans to homeowners. People say they will do it themselves, or ask for a lower price. Plans start at $540 a year.
We sell managed IT support to accounting firms with 10 to 40 staff. Objections: we have a nephew who does our IT, and it costs too much. Our contract is month to month.
Our school sells weekend coding classes for kids aged 9 to 14. Parents say: my child is too busy, or is it worth the money? We give a free first class.

demand_sources.note: Rate table by deliverable: email sequence $500 to $5,000, product description $25 to $250 each, case study $1,200 to $2,000, article $250 to $800.

title: Account research brief
summary: A one-page brief on a prospect company, built only from the notes and pages you give us.
deliverable: A brief per account: what they do, recent news you supplied, likely needs, who matters, three talking points, and questions to ask. Every point shows where it came from.

spec_fields.label: Paste what you know
spec_fields.help: Website text, news, LinkedIn text, call notes, their job posts.

spec_fields.label: Person you will talk to
spec_fields.help: Name and role.

spec_fields.label: Number of accounts
spec_fields.help: Paste material for each one.

rubric.text: Nothing is invented. Every fact about the prospect appears in the material the buyer pasted.
rubric.pass_rule: Each factual claim about the prospect can be found in source_material; anything else is clearly marked as a guess or a question.

rubric.text: Each fact points back to where it came from.
rubric.pass_rule: Facts carry a short source tag such as 'from the About page' or 'from your call notes'.

rubric.text: Guesses are labelled as guesses.
rubric.pass_rule: Likely needs and pains are labelled 'likely' or 'to check' and are not stated as fact.

rubric.text: The brief links the prospect to the buyer's offer.
rubric.pass_rule: At least three talking points connect a supplied fact to the buyer's offer.

rubric.text: It can be read in five minutes.
rubric.pass_rule: Each account brief is 500 words or fewer and starts with a three-line summary.

baseline_prompt: You are a sales researcher. Using only the notes and text I paste below, write a one-page account brief: what the company does, key facts, who matters, likely needs, three talking points tied to my offer, and questions to ask. Tag each fact with where it came from. Label guesses as guesses. Do not use any outside knowledge about the company and do not invent anything.
not_for: Looking up live data, since agents cannot browse for you
Personal or private details about individuals
Guessing numbers such as revenue or headcount

sample_briefs.text: Prospect: Harbor Dental Group. I pasted their About page and two job posts for hygienists. I sell online appointment reminders. I will talk to their office manager next Tuesday.
Prospect: Brightfield Farms, an organic produce grower. I pasted a press article about a new packing plant and notes from a trade show chat. We sell cold storage space by the pallet.

Prospect: Lindqvist & Moore, a 25-person law firm. I pasted their website and a LinkedIn post by a partner about hiring a legal assistant. We sell document automation. Goal: first call with the managing partner.
Prospects: three bike shops in Portland. I pasted each shop's website text. I sell a point of sale system built for bike shops. Brief each one.

demand_sources.note: Rate table by deliverable: email sequence $500 to $5,000, product description $25 to $250 each, case study $1,200 to $2,000, article $250 to $800.

title: Sales proposal
summary: A clear proposal for one prospect that sums up their problem, your plan, scope, price and next steps.
deliverable: A proposal with summary, the client's problem, your approach, scope and what is not included, timeline, pricing table, terms in plain words, and next steps.

spec_fields.label: Client name and what they do
Their problem and goals
spec_fields.help: Paste call notes or their request.

spec_fields.label: What you will do for them
Prices and payment terms
spec_fields.help: Give your real numbers. We do not guess prices.

spec_fields.label: Proof or past work you can cite

rubric.text: Nothing is invented. Prices, dates, results and past clients come from the brief.
rubric.pass_rule: Every price, date, deliverable, result and client name appears in the brief; missing details are shown as [to confirm], not made up.

rubric.text: It opens with the client's problem in their own terms.
rubric.pass_rule: The first section restates the client's problem and goals using details from the notes.

rubric.text: What is and is not included is clear.
rubric.pass_rule: The proposal lists deliverables and a separate list of what is not included, with no vague phrases like 'and more'.

rubric.text: Price, payment steps and what happens next are easy to find.
rubric.pass_rule: A pricing table matches the price_info field and the last section names the next step and who does it.

rubric.text: Terms are in plain words and do not pose as legal advice.
rubric.pass_rule: Terms are short bullets with no legal jargon, and the document says the buyer should have a lawyer review any contract.

baseline_prompt: You are an experienced consultant who writes winning proposals. Write a proposal for the client below using only my notes. Include an executive summary, the client's problem in their own words, my approach, scope with a clear list of what is not included, a timeline, a pricing table that uses only the prices I give, plain-language terms, and next steps. Where a detail is missing, write [to confirm]. Do not invent prices, dates, results or past clients.
not_for: Legal contracts or terms of service
Proposals with invented past work or testimonials
Pricing advice, since the buyer sets prices

sample_briefs.text: I run a small web design studio. A bakery owner wants a 5-page site with online ordering. I quoted $4,800: half now, half at launch. Build takes 5 weeks. Her call notes are below: she hates her current site, loses orders by phone, wants to take pre-orders for holidays.

Freelance bookkeeper. A landscaping firm with 12 employees wants monthly books, payroll reports and quarterly tax prep. My fee is $650 a month, three-month minimum. They use QuickBooks and are 4 months behind on reconciling.
We are a 3-person video team. A regional credit union wants 6 short training videos for new tellers. Quote: $9,500 for the set, 6 weeks, two rounds of edits per video. They supply the script outline.

I do HVAC installs. A small office building owner asked for a quote to replace two rooftop units. Price $31,200 including removal. Work takes 3 days over a weekend. Warranty is 5 years on parts from the maker.

demand_sources.note: Rate table by deliverable: email sequence $500 to $5,000, product description $25 to $250 each, case study $1,200 to $2,000, article $250 to $800.

title: Sales follow-up sequence
summary: Follow-up messages that keep a quote, demo or meeting moving without nagging.
deliverable: A set of follow-up emails or messages with timing, subject lines, and a short note on when to stop. Each message adds something new.

spec_fields.label: What happened so far
spec_fields.help: Paste notes or the last emails.

spec_fields.label: Proof or useful content to share

rubric.text: Nothing is invented. No fake deadlines, discounts, results or things the buyer 'said'.
rubric.pass_rule: No deadline, discount, number or quote appears that is not in the context or offer fields.

rubric.text: Messages refer to what actually happened in the deal.
rubric.pass_rule: At least half the messages mention a specific detail from the context field.

rubric.text: Each message adds something new.
rubric.pass_rule: No two messages share the same main reason for writing, and none is only 'just checking in'.

rubric.text: Each message makes the next step small and clear.
rubric.pass_rule: Each message has one ask that takes under five minutes, such as a yes or no reply.

rubric.text: The sequence ends well.
rubric.pass_rule: The last message is a polite close that leaves the door open, and the note says when to stop.

baseline_prompt: You are a sales coach. Write a follow-up sequence for the deal below. Give the timing, subject lines and message text for each touch. Refer to what really happened in the deal. Each message must add something new, not just check in, and must have one small ask. End with a polite breakup message and a note on when to stop. Use only the facts I give. Do not invent deadlines, discounts or results.
not_for: Fake urgency, fake deadlines or invented discounts
Harassing contacts who asked to stop
Bulk spam to people with no relationship

sample_briefs.text: We sent a $12,000 quote for a kitchen remodel 5 days ago. The homeowners liked our design but have not replied. They said money is a little tight. Need 4 follow-ups by email.
Two of us at a SaaS startup gave a demo to an operations director at a trucking firm last week. She said she needed to talk to her CFO. Our plan is $450 a month. I want 5 touches.
I own a photography studio. A couple asked about wedding packages in January and then went silent. Package prices start at $2,800. I want 3 gentle text messages.
Our free 14-day trial of an invoicing tool ended yesterday. The user created 8 invoices but did not upgrade. Plan costs $19 a month. Need a 3-email sequence.

demand_sources.note: Rate guide shows cold outreach at $100 to $350 per email and $300 to $1,000 per sequence. Cold outreach is one of the most-bought writing jobs.
Rate table by deliverable: email sequence $500 to $5,000, product description $25 to $250 each, case study $1,200 to $2,000, article $250 to $800.

title: Ideal customer profile
summary: A clear profile of the customers worth chasing, based on the customer facts you give us.
deliverable: An ideal customer profile with firmographics, buying triggers, pains, buyer roles, disqualifiers, where to find them, and how to score a lead.

spec_fields.label: Notes on your best customers
spec_fields.help: Who buys, why, how fast, how much. Paste a customer list or notes with names removed if you like.

spec_fields.label: Customers who were a poor fit

rubric.text: Nothing is invented. Facts about customers come from the notes; market numbers are not made up.
rubric.pass_rule: No statistic, customer detail or market size appears unless it is in the brief; inferences are labelled 'inferred'.

rubric.text: Each trait is tied to evidence in the customer notes.
rubric.pass_rule: Each major trait names the pattern in the notes that supports it, or says 'no evidence yet'.

rubric.text: The profile is specific enough to tell a good lead from a bad one.
rubric.pass_rule: It gives concrete firmographic traits, at least three buying triggers and at least three disqualifiers.

rubric.text: It includes a simple way to score a lead.
rubric.pass_rule: A scoring list of 5 to 10 yes-or-no checks is included with a rule for what score counts as a fit.

rubric.text: It says where and how to find these customers.
rubric.pass_rule: At least three places or ways to find the profile are listed, without scraped-list suggestions.

baseline_prompt: You are a B2B go-to-market strategist. From the customer notes below, write an ideal customer profile: firmographics, buying triggers, pains, roles in the buying group, disqualifiers, where to find these customers, and a simple lead scorecard. Tie each trait to evidence in my notes. Label inferences as inferred. Do not invent statistics or customer details.
not_for: Market size claims without a source from the buyer
Profiles based on protected traits such as race, religion or age of a person

sample_briefs.text: We sell route-planning software to small plumbing and HVAC companies. Our best 10 customers have 8 to 25 trucks, mostly family owned, and found us when fuel costs jumped. Poor fits: one-truck owners and big chains. Plan is $30 per vehicle per month.

I coach new managers in tech firms. My best clients are engineering directors at companies of 50 to 300 people, referred by their HR leads. They sign up after a reorg or a promotion. Price is $2,400 for a 6-week programme.
We make compostable packaging for takeaway restaurants. Best customers are independent cafes with 2 to 5 sites in cities that banned plastic. Chains buy from big suppliers and never replied.
My accounting practice serves online course creators earning $100k to $1M a year. They come after a surprise tax bill. Hobby creators below $30k a year do not stay.

demand_sources.note: Rate table by deliverable: email sequence $500 to $5,000, product description $25 to $250 each, case study $1,200 to $2,000, article $250 to $800.

title: Sales playbook
summary: A working playbook your reps can follow, built from how you actually sell today.
deliverable: A playbook with sales stages, entry and exit rules, questions per stage, email and call guides, objection list, qualification rules, and a first-week plan for new reps.

spec_fields.label: How you sell today
spec_fields.help: Steps from lead to signed deal, tools used, who does what.

spec_fields.label: Existing scripts or emails to build on

rubric.text: Nothing is invented. Stages, prices, rules and win rates come from the brief.
rubric.pass_rule: No price, discount rule, win rate, quota or tool appears that is not in the brief; gaps are listed as 'to decide'.

rubric.text: The stages match how the business really sells.
rubric.pass_rule: The stages follow the process field in order, and any new stage is marked 'suggested'.

rubric.text: Each stage has a goal, entry rule, exit rule and key questions.
rubric.pass_rule: Every stage lists all four items.

rubric.text: Reps get words they can use.
rubric.pass_rule: At least one email template, one call outline and one objection reply are included and tied to a stage.

rubric.text: New reps can get started from it.
rubric.pass_rule: A first-week plan with daily tasks is included.

baseline_prompt: You are a head of sales enablement. Using only the facts below, write a sales playbook: stages with a goal, entry rule, exit rule and key questions for each; qualification rules; email and call guides; common objections with replies; pricing and discount rules as given; and a first-week plan for new reps. Follow the sales process described. Mark anything missing as 'to decide'. Do not invent prices, quotas, win rates or tools.
not_for: Invented quotas, win rates or benchmarks
Playbooks for regulated sales such as insurance or investments

sample_briefs.text: We sell a $250 a month shift scheduling app to restaurants. Two reps. Leads come from Google ads. Steps today: web form, call within a day, 20-minute demo, 14-day trial, call at day 10, sign. We lose to a free app. We want a playbook for hiring a third rep.

Our firm installs security cameras for small retail stores. Owners call us, we visit, quote, and install in 2 weeks. Jobs range $2,500 to $9,000. Founder closes most deals. We want his method written down.
I run a 4-person agency selling monthly SEO retainers of $1,500 to $4,000 to local law firms. Sales cycle is 4 to 8 weeks. We win when we show a free site audit. We lose on price to cheap vendors.
We make custom uniforms and sell to schools and clubs. Orders open in spring. Reps are seasonal part-timers. Orders from $1,200 to $15,000. We need a playbook they can learn in a week.

demand_sources.note: Rate table by deliverable: email sequence $500 to $5,000, product description $25 to $250 each, case study $1,200 to $2,000, article $250 to $800.

title: Product descriptions in a batch
summary: Clear, accurate product descriptions for your online shop, written in one voice for the whole batch.
deliverable: One description per product with a short headline, a main description, key features as bullets, and a short meta description. Delivered in a table you can copy.

spec_fields.label: About your shop and brand voice
Product details
spec_fields.help: One product per block: name, materials, size, features, price if you like.

rubric.text: No feature, material, size, certification or claim is invented. Only the product details given are used.
rubric.pass_rule: Every fact in a description appears in that product's details; missing facts are listed as questions, not guessed.

rubric.text: Each description pairs real details with what they mean for the buyer.
rubric.pass_rule: Each description mentions at least two product facts and the benefit of each.

rubric.text: The whole batch reads in the voice of the shop.
rubric.pass_rule: Tone and sentence style match the shop field across all products, and no two descriptions share a repeated opening.

rubric.text: Each description fits the chosen length and format.
rubric.pass_rule: Word counts are within 15 percent of the chosen range, and every product has headline, description, bullets and meta description.

rubric.text: Plain, specific words with no empty hype.
rubric.pass_rule: No description uses words like 'amazing', 'perfect', 'luxurious' or 'must-have' without a fact beside it.

baseline_prompt: You are an ecommerce copywriter. Write a description for each product listed below, in the shop's voice. For each product give a short headline, a main description of the length requested, key features as bullets, and a meta description under 155 characters. Use only the product details I give. If something important is missing, list it as a question instead of guessing. Do not invent materials, sizes, certifications or claims. Avoid empty hype words and vary the openings.
not_for: Health, safety or eco claims the buyer cannot prove

sample_briefs.text: We sell handmade soy candles from a small studio in Vermont. 12 products. Each has a scent, burn time, jar size and wax type. Voice is calm and homey. I will paste the details for all 12.
Our shop sells men's work boots. I have 30 products with leather type, sole type, sizes and weight. Customers are tradespeople. Want medium-length descriptions, no hype.
Pet shop with 18 dog toys and 10 cat toys. Materials are listed for each. Some are made in Portugal. Tone is playful but clear about safety. We do not claim anything is indestructible.
We sell refurbished laptops. 15 listings, each with processor, RAM, storage, screen size, condition grade and battery health. Customers are students on a budget. Be clear about condition.

demand_sources.note: Copywriter pricing guide: product descriptions earn about $3 to $18 each at volume; worked example of $5 each.
Rate table by deliverable: email sequence $500 to $5,000, product description $25 to $250 each, case study $1,200 to $2,000, article $250 to $800.

title: Marketplace listing copy
summary: Title, bullets, description and search terms for listings on Amazon, Etsy, Shopify, eBay, Walmart or TikTok Shop.
deliverable: For each listing: a title, five bullets or highlights, a description, search terms or tags, and a list of questions about missing facts. Written to the rules of the chosen marketplace.

spec_fields.label: Product details
spec_fields.help: Materials, sizes, what is in the box, how it is used, care, origin.

spec_fields.label: Competing listings to beat (paste their text)
Rules you already know
spec_fields.help: Banned words, character limits, category rules.

rubric.text: No feature, certification, size, material or result is invented. Only given facts are used.
rubric.pass_rule: Every claim in the listing appears in the product field; certifications and 'best' or 'number one' claims appear only if the buyer supplied proof.

rubric.text: Format and length fit the chosen marketplace.
rubric.pass_rule: Title and bullets stay within the usual limits for the platform (Amazon title about 200 characters, Etsy title 140, Etsy tags 13 of 20 characters or fewer) or the limits the buyer gave.

rubric.text: Search words appear naturally in the title and early text.
rubric.pass_rule: The main search word appears in the title and in the first bullet or description line, with no stuffing or repeated word lists.

rubric.text: The listing answers what a buyer wants to know before buying.

rubric.text: Answers are short enough for a chat window.
rubric.pass_rule: Each answer is 60 words or fewer and starts with the answer.

rubric.text: Sensitive or unclear topics go to a person.
rubric.pass_rule: A handover list covers complaints, refunds above stated limits, legal, medical, safety and anything not in the facts, and says what the bot should say.

rubric.text: Entries do not conflict.
rubric.pass_rule: Times, prices and rules are the same wherever they appear across entries.

baseline_prompt: You are a conversation designer. Using only the source facts below, write knowledge base entries for a support chatbot. For each entry give three or more differently worded customer questions, a short answer (60 words or fewer, starting with the answer), and a handover rule if needed. Add a list of topics the bot must pass to a person, with the words the bot should use when doing so. Keep facts consistent. Do not invent prices, times or policies.
not_for: Answers that give legal, medical or financial advice
Making the bot pretend to be a human

sample_briefs.text: We run an online shop selling running gear. Cover shipping, returns, sizing, order tracking and discount codes. 50 entries. I pasted our policy pages and 40 past support emails.
Dental clinic with 3 locations. Chatbot should answer opening hours, booking, insurance questions (pass to staff) and what to do in an emergency (pass to phone). I pasted our site pages.
SaaS project tool. Cover pricing plans, free trial, integrations, importing data, and account deletion. 60 entries. Data protection questions go to a person.
Local council parking office. Cover permits, fines, appeals, where to pay and office hours. Appeals and anything about legal rights must go to staff. 40 entries from our website text.

title: Complaint response templates
summary: Calm, fair reply templates for upset customers, from small issues to serious complaints.
deliverable: Templates for common complaint types with a reply, a short guide for the agent on tone and limits, and a rule for when to pass a case to a manager.

spec_fields.label: What you can offer
spec_fields.help: Refunds, replacements, credits, who can approve.

rubric.text: No refund, credit, policy or time frame is invented. Replies offer only what the brief lists.
rubric.pass_rule: Every remedy and time frame matches the remedies field; none is promised beyond it.

rubric.text: Each reply shows the customer was heard before explaining.
rubric.pass_rule: The first two sentences acknowledge the specific problem and avoid generic apology phrases.

rubric.text: Each reply states the fix and what happens next.
rubric.pass_rule: Each template gives the remedy, who acts and when, using the brief.

rubric.text: No reply blames, argues or is sarcastic.
rubric.pass_rule: No reply puts blame on the customer or uses defensive wording.

rubric.text: Serious cases go to a person.
rubric.pass_rule: A rule lists when to escalate, including threats of legal action, safety issues and repeat complaints.

baseline_prompt: You are a customer experience manager. Write reply templates for the complaint types below. For each: the reply, a short note to the agent on tone and limits, and when to escalate. Acknowledge the specific problem first, state the fix and next step, and offer only the remedies I list. Do not blame the customer, be defensive, or promise anything outside my brief. Add a general escalation rule for legal threats, safety issues and repeat complaints.
not_for: Legal advice or replies to legal claims
Admitting fault for injuries or safety issues without approval
Threats or pressure on the customer

sample_briefs.text: We run a small airline-style shuttle service. Complaints: late pick-up, driver was rude, lost luggage, wrong booking. We can refund up to 50 percent for lateness. Manager approves more. Replies by email.

Online furniture shop. Complaints: item arrived damaged, delivery late, colour different from the photo, poor assembly instructions. We can send replacement parts or a full refund. Facebook comments need short replies.
Gym chain. Complaints: cancelled classes, dirty facilities, billing after cancelling. We can credit one month. Billing errors go to finance. Tone is respectful and brief.
Mobile phone repair shop. Complaints: repair took too long, same fault returned, price higher than quote. Free redo within 30 days. Price disputes go to the owner.

title: Support quality review
summary: A scored review of support conversations you paste in, with coaching points for your team.
deliverable: A scorecard per conversation, patterns across all of them, strengths, top fixes, better sample replies, and training points for the team.

spec_fields.label: Support conversations
spec_fields.help: Paste tickets or chat transcripts. Remove names, emails and card details first.

spec_fields.label: Your support standards
spec_fields.help: Tone rules, reply time targets, policy limits.

rubric.text: Nothing is invented. Every finding quotes or points to the supplied conversations.
rubric.pass_rule: Each finding cites a conversation by number and quotes or paraphrases a line that is in it; no statistic is invented.

rubric.text: Scores follow a clear scorecard.
rubric.pass_rule: A scorecard with defined categories and a scoring rule is shown, and every conversation is scored with a short reason.

rubric.text: It finds patterns across conversations.
rubric.pass_rule: At least three patterns are named, each with the conversation numbers that show it.

rubric.text: Coaching is specific and kind.
rubric.pass_rule: Each top fix includes a better sample reply or wording that uses only policy facts from the brief.

rubric.text: It handles private data with care.
rubric.pass_rule: The review does not repeat personal data such as full names, emails or card numbers found in the transcripts.

baseline_prompt: You are a support quality analyst. Review the support conversations I paste below. Give each a score using a clear scorecard (tone, accuracy, policy, clarity, resolution) with a one-line reason. Then list patterns across the conversations with the conversation numbers, strengths, the top fixes with better sample replies, and coaching points for the team. Quote or cite the conversation for every finding. Do not invent statistics and do not repeat personal data.
not_for: Judging or ranking individual staff for pay or firing decisions
Transcripts with unredacted card numbers or health data

sample_briefs.text: Here are 20 chat transcripts from our online shop's support team of 3. I want to see tone problems, wrong policy answers and missed chances to fix the problem on the first reply. Our policy: refunds within 30 days.
I pasted 12 email threads from our SaaS support. Our target is a first reply in under 4 hours and a clear next step in every reply. Please score each and give coaching points for two new agents.
30 customer calls turned into text for our home repair booking line. Standards: confirm the address and time, never promise a price over the phone. Focus on accuracy and escalations.
Here are 15 tickets about refunds from our online course. Many customers write twice. I want to know why and what to change in the replies.

title: Feedback and NPS comment analysis
summary: Themes, counts and action points drawn from the customer comments and survey answers you paste in.
deliverable: A report with top themes and counts, sample quotes, what promoters and detractors say, a ranked list of fixes, and a short summary you can share with your team.

spec_fields.label: Customer comments
spec_fields.help: Paste survey answers, reviews or tickets. Remove names and contact details.

spec_fields.label: NPS or rating scores, if you have them
spec_fields.help: Paste score counts or a list of score and comment pairs.

rubric.text: Nothing is invented. Every theme, count and quote comes from the pasted comments.
rubric.pass_rule: Counts add up to the supplied comments, every quote appears verbatim in the input, and no score or percentage is shown that cannot be worked out from the data.

rubric.text: Themes are clear and not overlapping.
rubric.pass_rule: Themes have short names, a count, and at least two example quotes each.

rubric.text: The method is shown.
rubric.pass_rule: The report says how comments were grouped and how many comments fit no theme.

rubric.text: The fixes are ranked and specific.
rubric.pass_rule: Each fix links to a theme, says who should act and why it is ranked where it is.

rubric.text: The report does not overclaim from few comments.
rubric.pass_rule: Themes with fewer than 5 comments are labelled low evidence, and no trend is claimed without data to compare.

baseline_prompt: You are a customer insights analyst. Analyse the customer comments I paste below. Group them into themes with counts and at least two verbatim example quotes each. Say what promoters and detractors talk about if scores are given. Rank fixes by how many customers raise them. Explain how you grouped comments and how many did not fit a theme. Label themes with few comments as low evidence. Do not invent numbers, quotes or trends.
not_for: Statistical claims the data cannot support

sample_briefs.text: I pasted 180 answers to 'What could we do better?' from our online yoga studio's survey. NPS was 41 last quarter. Please find top themes and what we should fix first.
Here are 90 app store reviews of our budgeting app, rating 1 to 5. I want themes by star rating and what to fix in the next release.
Hotel guest comments, 250 of them from the last 3 months, with scores from 0 to 10. Please compare what promoters and detractors mention and rank problems by how often they come up.
We ran a survey for our B2B accounting software. 60 comments are pasted, from small firms and larger firms. Compare the two groups and tell us if the data is too small to say.
